subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTH OF SON

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTH OF SON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members heard yesterday with great pleasure the happy news from Buckingham palace, and would wish this House of Commons to send a message of congratulations and loyalty to the Queen, and of good wishes, good fortune and long life to the baby prince. Perhaps also, Mr. Speaker, we should not forget the man who is so often forgotten on these occasions, Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh.
We rejoice with Her Majesty, thinking of her both as the Queen of Canada and head of the commonwealth, to whom we owe loyalty, and also as a gracious and lovely lady to whom we gladly give our respect and affection. The Queen, as wife and mother, exemplifies all that is finest and best in family life at a time when there are so many pressures undermining the solidarity and health of the family as the essential foundation of communal and national life.
The Queen also, as head of the commonwealth, symbolizes the full association, the free association, of many peoples of diverse colours, creeds and cultures from the four corners of the world in a commonwealth of nations.
Finally, as Queen of Canada as well as of Britain she is a living reminder of the depth of our roots and the continuity of our history. The monarchy thus adds strength and stability to our national development without detracting in any way from our democratic and our national freedom. It is well to remind ourselves of these things when so many of our institutions and traditions are under challenge and attack. But today we are thinking primarily of the Queen as a happy mother with a new baby.
I therefore move, seconded by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition:
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To Her Most Excellent Majesty Elizabeth the Second, by the grace of God of the United Kingdom, Canada and her other Realms and Territories! Queen, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith:

Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's Commons of Canada, in par' liament assembled, respectfully desire to offer our loyal and warm congratulations to Your Majesty and His Royal Highness the Prince Philip on the birth of a son. and to assure Your Majesty that this happy event gives the members of the House of Commons of Canada great joy and satisfaction.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTH OF SON
speechtext:
I am very happy to join with the Prime Minister in this motion, for the birth of the infant prince touches the feelings of us all, not only in our country but in countries in all parts of the world within the commonwealth. Her Majesty has given a life of service to her peoples everywhere while at the same time maintaining, as the Prime Minister has said, the happiness and joy of an exemplary family life. I express the hope, as did the Prime Minister, that the young prince's life will be one of happiness and service in a world at peace.
I think, too, that at this time the Queen should know that this message is not a perfunctory one but rather that it represents the heartfelt sentiments of her Canadian people. She will also want to know that however strident the babble of a minute minority may be, she, as Queen of Canada, and her husband the Prince Philip will be welcomed with loyalty, devotion and genuine affection when she visits her realm of Canada later this year.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTH OF SON
speechtext:
Members of this party desire to associate themselves with the sentiments expressed in the motion moved by the Prime Minister and seconded by the Leader of the Opposition. In these troubled times the commonwealth has had a stabilizing influence in world affairs. This commonwealth of free nations is held together by a common loyalty to the crown, to our traditions of equality before the law and our parliamentary institutions. For those of us in the commonwealth, the crown and the monarchy have come to symbolize these institutions and these long held traditions.
For this reason we are glad to associate ourselves with this expression of loyalty and affection. We wish to convey to Her Majesty and to His Royal Highness Prince Philip our heartiest congratulations, and to the newborn prince our best wishes for a long, happy and useful life.

speechtext:
Personally, Mr. Speaker, and on behalf of the members of our party I am pleased indeed to share in the expression of joy and good will

Congratulations to Queen being made by this house to Her Majesty the Queen. Events such as this make us realize that our commonwealth is not simply a form of government organization, even though one of the greatest heritages we have from it is the parliamentary form of government, for which each one of us individually in this house has a personal responsibility. Our commonwealth provides a much stronger bond, the bond of family relationship where the joys and sorrows of one member are those of all. We thank God for Her Majesty's safe delivery, and hope that in the years to come Canada and the commonwealth will be well served by our new prince.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTH OF SON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I gladly join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in extending our best wishes to Her Majesty the Queen who has given birth to her fourth child, and wish them both good health and long life.
If Her Majesty the Queen is for many people a mere symbol of the crown, I must say that for us she represents a loving mother who brings forth children for her country. In this morning's edition of a Montreal newspaper I saw a picture of the Queen decked out in all her finery. I could not help thinking of the thousands of Canadian mothers who can only manage to buy clothes with social security allowances and unemployment insurance benefits. Yet, they also give birth to little Canadian princes who tomorrow will have to face the economic problems of the country.
If royalty is threatened in some part of the empire, I must say that the subjects are threatened in several parts of our country.
At any rate, I hope that the respect and love inspired by our Queen will enable our authorities to understand better their duties towards the people under their administration.

MR. VALADE  STATEMENT BY FORMER TORONTO MAYOR RESPECTING ROMAN CATHOLIC CLERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It concerns a matter affecting all Roman Catholic members of this house, as well as the 10 million Canadians of Roman Catholic faith in this country.
My question of privilege rises from a statement made a few days ago by a former mayor of Toronto called Saunders. His statement was brought to my knowledge today only. This then is the first opportunity given me to bring up this question in the house.
As reported in the March 10, 1964 edition of La Presse, the remarks made by this former mayor would have the public believe that the Roman Catholic clergy is responsible for the wave of separatism.
I quote Mr. Saunders:
The Catholic clergy sowed the seeds of discord when they established missions on our continent.
I wish to object strongly to such claims which border on hysteria, if not pure and simple madness.
History gives clear evidence of the fact that if it had not been for the Roman Catholic clergy, lower Canada would have joined with American revolutionaries instead of standing with British forces to fight against the American invasion early in our history.
The Roman Catholic clergy has always been loyal and respectful of established authority. No member of the Catholic clergy made any statement as seditious as the one made by the former mayor of Toronto.
As a Roman Catholic and a member of parliament coming from a province where the population is Roman Catholic in a proportion of 80 per cent, I consider Mr. Saunders' statement as a personal insult and I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), to have an examination made of that person's statement in order to take criminal proceedings if they are considered to be of a seditious nature.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA, OUTLOOK 1964"

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA, OUTLOOK 1964"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have today tabled a report "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1964", containing the results of a recent survey of capital expenditure intentions. The survey covers business establishments, institutions, government and new housing. In view of the fact that my colleague the Minister of Finance will be bringing down his budget on Monday and will shortly be tabling his white paper, I thought I should indicate to the house the general results of this report.
The report indicates that total capital outlays of $10.1 billion are planned for
Statement on Royal Visit 1964. This figure exceeds actual outlays in 1963 by 8 per cent compared with increases of 7 per cent in each of the two preceding years.
More than half of the expected gross in total private and public investment is by the business community. Within the major business groups the sharpest expansion is indicated in manufacturing, where spending intentions for 1964 provide for an increase of 15 per cent compared with actual outlays in 1963. Manufacturing industries planning to have sharply increased programs under way in 1964 include pulp and paper, iron and steel, cement, transportation equipment, rubber and textiles. Higher outlays are also planned in mining, transportation, electric power, retail trade and in several other business sectors.
Within the institutional field larger spending programs are indicated for university and hospital facilities, but outlays for schools will be below the 1963 level, reflecting the advanced stage of the large technical school building program. Expanded provincial road construction programs are the major factor contributing to the 8 per cent increase in government projects. A substantial carryover of unfinished houses into the current year is expected to result in a further growth in house building activity.
Outlays for new construction and machinery and equipment in each ease are expected to be up by 8 per cent. Programs of this magnitude will entail increased activity in both the construction trades and equipment producing industries, and should provide an important stimulus to the economy generally.

subtopic: ADVICE TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING TRIP TO CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ADVICE TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING TRIP TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the Leader of the Opposition asked me certain questions about the invitation extended to Her Majesty to visit Prince Edward Island and Quebec. I said I would make a statement dealing with the background of the arrangements, and I am glad to do that now.
The question of a visit by Her Majesty to coincide with the centennial celebrations in Quebec city and Charlottetown appears first to have been raised in a letter of March 30, 1961, from the lieutenant governor of Prince Edward Island to His Excellency the Governor General. The lieutenant governor said that his government had asked him to forward an invitation to Her Majesty the Queen to be

Statement on Royal Visit present at the commemoration that was being planned for the historic meeting held in Charlottetown in 1864.
The matter was, of course, referred by the Governor General to the government of the day, who considered it in relation to plans being made both to commemorate the events of 1864 and the centennial of confederation itself. The then government decided in November, 1962 that a royal visit in 1964, which would include Quebec city and Charlottetown, would be appropriate if Her Majesty found it possible, as centennial celebrations would be taking place in those cities in 1964. The government was then advised in November, 1962 that the Queen would not be able to consider invitations for 1964 much before the autumn of 1963.
On September 25, 1963 the premier of Prince Edward Island wrote to me and, with reference to previous discussions, raised again the question of the invitation to the Queen. In a letter of November 5 to the premier I inquired as to the dates that might be most appropriate for Charlottetown, having in mind certain arrangements that Her Majesty was understood to have for the autumn of this year, that is 1964. Premier Shaw answered on November 21 indicating that if the exact anniversary of the Charlottetown conference was not possible, the most suitable time would be early in October.
As the federal-provincial conference was to begin a day or two after I got this letter, I felt that the best course would be to discuss the matter with Premier Shaw and Premier Lesage before extending any formal invitation. This I did on the evening of November 27 while they were here in Ottawa. The premiers of Quebec and Prince Edward Island both indicated their desire that an invitation should be extended. I then wrote formally to the Governor General on December 5 to advise him of this, and to ask that his office take the appropriate action to ascertain whether Her Majesty and the Duke of Edinburgh would be able to visit Charlottetown and Quebec in the autumn of 1964.
This was done and, as a result, the invitation was extended in the appropriate way through the office of the Governor General to Her Majesty to visit both Prince Edward Island and Quebec on the dates agreed upon. The invitation was accepted in a letter from the palace in London, dated December 24.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that I was in error when I said on Monday that I thought the fact of the visit had been announced in the house. I had forgotten that the acceptance came after the house had adjourned last December. The actual announcement was made in the

proper way from Government House on January 27 of this year. The text of that announcement was as follows:
It is announced from Government House that the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh have accepted the invitation of the government of Canada to attend special centennial celebrations in October commemorating the visits of the fathers of confederation to Charlottetown and Quebec city in 1864. The visit will begin in Charlottetown about October 6 and end in Quebec about October 12.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: HAY RIVER, N.W.T.  CURTAILMENT OF TEACHING SERVICE
speechtext:
Grade 12 has not been taught at Hay River for several years because of the very small potential enrolment, and will not be taught in 1964-65. Pupils are accommodated at the Sir John Franklin school in Yellowknife.
Because of the small enrolment in grades 10 and 11, a high school program fully satisfactory for matriculation requirements cannot be offered. Mr. Speaker, on March 6 the hon. member for Greenwood asked me to comment on the propriety of a letter said to have been sent to senior air force officers by the chief of the air staff, having in mind what the hon. member described as the salutary tradition of civilian control over the military. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CYPRUS'-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the crisis that threatens the authority of the United Nations, and in view of the fact that Canadians generally would welcome any statement which would indicate that

Canada is prepared to do its utmost to maintain the prestige of the United Nations, is the minister prepared to make a more firm and definite statement than he made yesterday to the effect that Canada will send troops to Cyprus to be part of a peace keeping United Nations force, in the event that the conditions set forth by the Prime Minister are complied with?
Hon, Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition sent me a note a few moments ago and I think I should, in responding to this question, indicate that he had in mind a question along these lines. In answer I would say, as I have already said, there should be no doubt. Canada does not intend to shirk its responsibilities under the charter of the United Nations. We continue to be ready to participate in a truly international United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus.
So far as Canada is concerned, responsibility for financing our force is not an obstacle. While the financing of the proposed force is not a key question in so far as this country is concerned, it is a key factor in respect of other potential contributing nations. It is regrettable that a consideration of this nature should have such a central place in determining whether or not the United Nations is able to meet its peace keeping responsibilities in situations where a failure to act could have such dire consequences. Nevertheless, that is the main remaining obstacle to the creation of a multinational United Nations force. All the secretary general's efforts are now being concentrated on the creation of a fund to be raised by voluntary contribution, from which could be met those costs which certain potential contributor states feel unable to meet from their national resources.

subtopic: CYPRUS'-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I take it from the minister's remarks that if the other nations which have been asked to contribute forces can be satisfied in respect of the financial costs involved and that difficulty is removed, Canada will be prepared to send troops to be part of a multinational United Nations peace keeping force?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CYPRUS'-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes.

subtopic: CYPRUS'-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE

Has the attention of the Prime Minister been drawn to the fact that a bill has been introduced in the Swedish parliament to establish by law the organization of an armed force to be available for the United Nations
Inquiries of the Ministry for peace keeping purposes, and that two other Scandinavian countries are going to do the same thing within the next two months? If so, has the Prime Minister considered the introduction into this house of a bill smilar in principle, and also co-ordinating our peace keeping force for the United Nations with those Scandinavian countries which want to do this by law?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CYPRUS'-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no such bill is required, because that is the situation in regard to this country at the present time. This situation existed under the previous government as well as this government, namely that a force would be available, trained and equipped, for United Nations service. Perhaps my hon. friend will recall that at the last assembly of the United Nations the Canadian delegation made a plea for other countries to take the same steps; if they would follow the example of those members of the United Nations who had taken this action, we could get together and work out a standby United Nations force on a broader than national basis. The Scandinavian states are now working this out.
My hon. friend has mentioned the bill being introduced in the Swedish legislature. We have already been in touch with these Scandinavian states and I hope we can get in touch with other countries that will take the same action. Then we will have a United Nations force ready for the kind of action that is required, for instance, in Cyprus today, and we will not be faced with the difficulties with which we are faced today.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickers-gill (for the Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the re-adjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such representation in accordance therewith.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out immediately to the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) that I shall be brief. I merely wish to set out a few of the underlying principles which should govern our conduct in the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions.
I know that in theory everyone seems more or less in favour of the democratic principle of representation by population and that we all want every man's vote to have the same weight as that of any other Canadian, taking into consideration a certain margin of tolerance.
That is a democratic principle which should be respected but I feel that we should also take into account other institutional considerations-if I may use that word-and by that I mean the occupation of the voters and the geographical and topographical characteristics of the ridings.
In my case, I represent a rather heavily populated riding which, fortunately, consists of people from different walks of life. It is a riding which could be called semi-urban and semi-rural, which gives one the opportunity to know the opinion of people from rural and urban areas.
Obviously, the point of view of farmers is not quite the same as that of the factory workers or the people employed in cities and towns. Their problems are not the same and they should be able to rely on members, maybe in lesser number than those representing urban areas, but anyway quite representative of their area.
If we take, for instance, the city of Montreal, which is very heavily populated and represented at present by 21 members. We see that the voters are not interested too much in politics.
It may no doubt be said they are not interested because they do not feel they have enough members. That may be true. But looking upon the past, we realize rather that the bigger the cities, the bigger the communities, the smaller the interest of people in public affairs and the greater their feeling of remoteness from the administration of democracy.
That is why, despite all the respect we may possibly have for the principles of democracy,
I believe this peculiarity of the people living in urban centres should be taken into account.
I should also like to make a brief comment on section 51 of the British North

Electoral Boundaries Commissions America Act. Taking that section as it appeared in 1867, we realize that, according to the spirit of the constitution-perhaps not in the spirit which moved Lower Canada at the time to grant that privilege to the province of Quebec or Lower Canada, but in the spirit in which Lower Canada accepted this condition-the number of members for the province of Quebec was set at 65. Since then, some changes have been made, so that, now, the province of Quebec is entitled to 75 constituencies.
I think we should revert to that spirit which inspired the enactment of the British North America Act and decide that the province of Quebec should continue to have at least 75 constituencies, irrespective of the total population of the province and irrespective of the ratio between the population of the province of Quebec and that of Canada and the other provinces. And this for several reasons, especially nowadays when we speak about bilingualism, the French fact and the two nations forming the country.
As the province of Quebec really represents the French element in Canada, I believe it should be assured to have never less than 75 constituencies, should the number of members be kept at 265, and the bill makes no mention of a change in that regard. In my opinion, as long as the province remains within confederation, it would be a good safeguard for Quebec to have a guaranteed minimum representation of 75 members.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say one last word concerning the choice of the people who will sit on each of the provincial electoral boundaries commissions. I am sure there must be a non-partisan way of making appointments. The hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) also spoke about this yesterday.
Each submitted proposals which could be acceptable but which would entail some difficulties in the constitutional field or as regards federal and provincial responsibilities.
If everyone would try and find some means to remove any possible political interference in the selection of the commissioners, I feel that we would be making real progress.
It should not be forgotten that parties change. We hope that in a more or less near future, we will have new parties instead of the two old ones. But they will be liable to change. Consequently, if a party resorts to political expediency, when another party comes into power, the latter will profit by it.
All things considered, it is surely possible to find an adequate method of appointing commissioners entirely free from any political affiliation.
[Mr. Marcoux.l
Mr. Speaker, I shall say no more for now. We shall have an opportunity to deal further with this bill when it is studied in committee. But I wanted to point out to the house in particular certain principles which should guide our discussions on this bill, because they represent logical and justifiable ideas for which every one of us, under a democratic system, will have to fight in order to preserve them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
As
has been said by others who have taken part in this debate, the bill before us now is one of tremendous significance. It will, undoubtedly, in future years be regarded as one of two historic landmarks in the history of redrawing constituency boundaries in this country.
The first landmark, at least in my opinion, was in 1903 when the government of that day under Sir Wilfrid Laurier decided to refer this task to an all-party committee of the House of Commons, rather than have the boundaries drawn by the cabinet and pushed through the house in the same way as ordinary bills.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Are you sure it was a change?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes. There had been, prior to 1903, three redistributions, those of 1872, 1882, and 1892, and in all these cases the government of the day had decided on the allotment, drawn the constituency boundaries and pushed its decisions through the house by means of its majority. This brought about colossal gerrymanders, in particular the famous gerrymander of 1882.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Tell us about Lake Centre.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think Professor Dawson says that some 46 constituencies in Ontario alone were gerrymandered in 1882. What the legislation of 1903 did was to transfer the problem to a select committee of the house in which other political parties would have more opportunity than formerly to air their complaints, and try to secure as fair a redistribution as possible. As a result of the new method they were able to exercise a greater influence on the final decisions and, indeed, after 1903 there was none of the really colossal gerrymandering that Canada had experienced before.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: You don't mean it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
It is quite true. According to every Canadian historian, both Conservative and Liberal, there was nothing to compare with the three Tory gerrymanders of 1872, 1882 and 1892.

The second important change, and it is of course an even greater change, is the one we are discussing today, namely that decisions in the matter of redistributing electoral boundaries should be taken out of the hands of a special committee of the house and placed in the hands of an impartial commission or commissions. This is, of course, almost a revolutionary step for this country, at any rate, to take although, as we all know, it has been done in other countries. The question whether or not redistribution should be placed in the hands of one national commission or a series of ten commissions, one for each province is, I think, not a particularly thorny one. I say this because there is general agreement, I think, on the desirability of having one commission in charge of redistribution for each province. The argument in favour of doing so is a strong one, bearing in mind the time which would be involved if we were to proceed in any other way, and the need to have people sitting on these bodies who are reasonably familiar with the characteristics of their own provinces.
I have no doubt that under the proposal in the bill the commission would be thoroughly impartial, but to make it appear to be completely so I agree with other hon. members that we should, if possible-as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has already tried to do-find some other means of appointing the two additional members of each provincial commission. I think we all agree that in each case the chairman should be appointed by the chief justice of the province concerned; but what about the other two members? The proposal was made yesterday that one way to make the appointments of the other two and place the emphasis on the office rather than the person would be to try to follow the Australian example, where the appointments to the six state commissions are by virtue of office.
I would point out, however-indeed the Minister of Transport has already pointed this out in part-that this is difficult because our federal government does not really have the authority to require certain provincial officials to perform a particular task. One reason it works in Australia is that there they have joint rolls and have for some time had a working relationship between the states and the federal government on the matter of voters lists and redistribution. They have developed a kind of co-operative federalism in the area having to do with both state and federal voting. Should we ever adopt permanent voters lists in this country and use joint rolls, I think it would be quite possible that we too could establish some kind of commission by office, appointing provincial officers to those commissions and having this
Electoral Boundaries Commissions written into the federal statute concerned. But probably until that time comes it is, as has been said before, rather difficult for a federal statute to require a provincial official to do a certain job.
There is a second objection, which is that in Canada the surveyors general, for example, in the different provinces are not all officials. In one instance I can thing of this person is a minister of the crown, or perhaps there are two instances. Nor indeed are they always appointed under a civil service commission; they may be politically appointed. For that reason also the suggestion that we follow the Australian practice is not entirely workable. In Australia, all the officials, the commonwealth electoral officers, the state electoral officers, the surveyors general, and so on, are officials under the civil service commission.
My suggestion, for what it is worth, on the question of how one should appoint the other two members of the provincial commissions is that officials under federal jurisdiction should be asked to make these appointments; one to make one set of appointments to the provincial commissions, and the other to make the other set. I would think that the two officials one might choose- although there would be others, perhaps, whom we could consider-who would be logical persons to ask to perform this task would be the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada and the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada. This would mean that each of the ten commissions would consist of the appointee of the chief justice of the province, one person appointed by the chief justice of Canada and a third person appointed by the president of the exchequer court. The fourth person on each commission would, of course, be the representation commissioner. We could perhaps go further and draw up in a schedule the offices among which the two appointments in each case might be made. Certainly where it was at all feasible it would be desirable that the chief electoral officer of each province should be on the provincial commission in question.
There may be other suggestions. Some people have been talking-not in this house, but elsewhere-about the possibility of having the chief justice of each province, or the representation commissioner, make the other two appointments. Perhaps there is some value in that suggestion. At any rate, my view is that if possible, since this is a federal statute, we should have two officials under federal jurisdiction, perform this task. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that this suggestion might raise some comment in debate, I should like to suggest that these

Electoral Boundaries Commissions two people be the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada and the president of the exchequer court.
Then we come to the question which has been arousing a good deal of discussion, and rightly so. This is the question of tolerance. I suggested at the beginning of my remarks that one of the reasons this bill is such an important constitutional landmark is that it removes redistribution from political partisanship, or partisan wrangling. But the second reason for its being a tremendous historical landmark is that for the first time we are really going to get at this problem of disparities between our various constituencies. No matter what the tolerance is, even if it went as high as 40 per cent-and I may say I find that only with 40 per cent would there be any hope of the boundaries of my riding remaining unchanged-it would still be, under this bill, an enormous change from the past. Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will not mind my putting one or two statistics on the record concerning this point, so that we will see as vividly as we can what a very great change this bill does represent in overcoming the disparities, even if there is a fairly wide tolerance.
Today, for example, in the province of Ontario the populations of the constituencies represented in the federal house vary from approximately 29,000 to approximately 267,000; that is to say, the population of the largest seat is about nine times larger than that of the smallest seat. The same is true of every other province in Canada. In some cases the disparities are even greater. In one case the population of the largest seat is more than 20 times greater than that of the smallest. Let us consider the suggestion of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) of a 33J per cent tolerance. That would bring down the disparity to, at the most, having the population of one seat twice the size of another. Personally I am impressed by this terrific change. In Ontario, if one introduces a 33 J per cent tolerance, the range, the disparity, instead of being from 29,000 to 267,000 would be from 47.2 thousand to 94.4 thousand.
I just want to impress, particularly on my urban friends, what a very great difference this is. With a 20 per cent tolerance the disparity would be even narrower. With a 20 per cent tolerance and I am speaking again of Ontario, where the quotient is 70.8 thousand- the smallest figure would be 56.6 thousand, and the largest would be 84.9 thousand. So that whether we take the 33i per cent or the 20 per cent tolerance, or indeed go down to 10 per cent as some have suggested, it seems to me not really as significant or as important. The differences between 10, 20 and 33J are
IMiss Jewett.]
not really all that substantial. What is really significant about this legislation is that it is for the first time going to cut into these mammoth disparities which have existed in this country for a very long period of time.
Another point which frequently is not made sufficiently clear in connection with the disparities which exist, is that many of them are found between urban seats. Sometimes when I listen to the debate in this house on this subject I get the feeling that it is a kind of urban versus rural fight, that the urban seats are all great, large burgeoning seats, and that all the rural seats are small in terms of population. In fact, of course, this is not the case at all.
Let us take, for example, Toronto. In a city like Toronto there are almost as sharp disparities between one urban seat and another as there are between some rural seats and some urban seats. The constituency of Rose-dale, for instance, at the 1961 census had a population of 56,015, whereas York-Scarbor-ough, our favourite population contest winner, had 267,252. Rosedale is a little over 56,000, whereas York-Scarborough is a little over 267,000. Similarly St. Paul's in Toronto, which is situated in the corporate part of the city, had a population of 53,155 in 1961, whereas York Centre, one of the suburban metropolitan constituencies, had 190,405.
The same is true in Montreal. For example, in the constituency of St. Ann there were 38,173 people, whereas in Mercier there were 233,964. The constituency of Laurier had a population of 45,652, whereas Laval, also in Montreal, had 193,437. And so one could go on. There is a difference between Carleton at 130,497 and Ottawa East, one of its neighbours, at 51,828. Even Edmonton East and Edmonton West show a sharp disparity, one being almost twice the size of the other.
As I say, one of the points which will help remove this constant urban-rural conflict, and which should perhaps have been discussed more, is the realization that the disparities between the urban seats are very sharp indeed. One of the important things which this bill will do is iron out the worst of these disparities. Indeed, I see no reason why there need be any great disparity between one urban seat and another. One could argue that in urban areas which can be determined to be fast-growth areas there might be some logic in that kind of seat in the suburbs-although it would be very difficult to do this-not being made quite as large initially as a seat in the core of the city.

speechtext:
Might I ask just one question. As a matter of interest there is in some

instances quite a population shift back into the centre of cities, or parts of cities which are not the suburbs.

speechtext:
Of course there is a population shift, but nothing compared with the much more substantial increase in the suburbs. Therefore there might be some ground for arguing that the suburban metro seats have slightly fewer people than the core seats. But by and large, unless one gets a pretty scientific estimate of probable population trends and growth rates it seems to me desirable to have our urban seats roughly the same in size. This is one of the biggest things we need which would resolve a good deal of the problem raised by such constituencies as the one the hon. member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. Moreau) represents. I realize he always tends to compare his constituency with a rural seat, but in comparison with other urban seats he is pretty badly underrepresented too.
If my arithmetic is correct, if the quotient for Ontario is 70,800 persons per seat, and if the tolerance is 20 per cent, the core of Toronto-that is, the corporate old city- would lose two seats. Suburban Toronto, the York ridings, would gain five seats. That means there would be a net gain-and here I am not using the full 20 per cent tolerance -of about three seats for the whole of metropolitan Toronto, because of the fact that there is a major readjustment which must be carried out within the city itself. The same is true of Montreal, Ottawa, Edmonton and other cities in Canada.
Should there, then, also be no disparities from one rural seat to another? One could argue here too that there is no reason for there being a sharp disparity between one rural seat and another. However, I think we should remember that some rural seats could be more properly described as hinterland seats. They are not really farming or agricultural constituencies, but they are very large indeed in geographic terms. It seems to me that these constituencies should be at the minimum level allowed under the act. We should not attempt, in other words, to have them roughly the same size as the average rural seat.
Then we come to the question which has been most discussed, namely what differential there should be between urban seats on the one hand and rural or hinterland seats on the other. The first think I should say on this, a point which has not yet been made, is that probably every constituency in Canada will be changed. There is a tendency for us to look at our constituencies from where we sit and say to ourselves: "Let me see, my population is so and so; I guess I am going to be within the tolerance"-whether it be
Electoral Boundaries Commissions 20 per cent or 33J-"and I will be o.k." This of course, will not be the case. The population of some constituencies will not change very much; however, its borders may change a very great deal. It may take in some other area and lose a part it formerly had. Indeed, this is one of the major features to which I do not think hon. members have yet adjusted their minds. One of the greatest certainties about this piece of legislation is that it will involve a comprehensive, over-all look at all constituencies in each province, not from the point of view of the members or the local politicians but from an over-all point of view based on reasonably scientific criteria. Therefore, there is nothing to prevent a fairly sharp change in constituency boundaries. Yours or mine may be cut in two or it may disappear entirely.
Furthermore, much as we would like, there can certainly be no rigid adherence to county lines.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) made a strong plea, one that has been heard many times in the house and with which I have a good deal of sympathy, that if possible we should not carve up the counties. In fact, however, this has never been possible in the past and is even less likely in this new redistribution. What is terribly important, of course, is that we do not carve up the municipalities. Every effort should be made to follow municipal boundaries, and this is perhaps one of the main reasons why we need a tolerance of at least 20 per cent.
It seems to me that there are several good reasons why rural ridings should be somewhat smaller in population than urban ridings. One good reason that is frequently given, and which was given yesterday, is that the member of parliament for a rural riding -in my case my riding is about three quarters rural-receives a larger number of requests for help and information than does an urban member, the kind of requests that in an urban area go to the local district office of the department of government concerned. One can easily determine this kind of thing by comparing notes with one's fellows from urban areas.
I do not believe, however, that this argument alone should be sufficient to keep rural ridings smaller in population than urban ones. It seems to me that what we really need as members of parliament, especially those of us who find that we spend practically all of our time coping with requests from our constituents, quite legitimate requests but ones which often take a great deal of time to obtain the information and to answer, is an executive assistant or two. Therefore the real answer to this problem is

Electoral Boundaries Commissions not to distort the electoral system but to provide more assistance to those members of parliament who receive an enormous amount of correspondence from their constituents.
When I was in Washington in January with other hon. members participating in the interparliamentary talks I was amazed, and I am sure others were as well, to discover that a member of the house of representatives, the lower house of the United States congress, who is elected for a two year term, has a staff of approximately seven. The number varies, depending on how active the member is and what kind of district he represents. But one in particular, whom we all got to know quite well, had five assistants in Washington and two in his district, all paid for by the government.

speechtext: We are only peasants here.

speechtext:
Mind you, the United States is a very wealthy country and no doubt can afford a good deal of help for its elected representatives. However, if each member of our parliament had even one assistant it would help us in the matter of looking after the needs, which are very great indeed, of rural and hinterland types of constituencies, and we need this help both in Ottawa and in our constituencies.
There are, however, two main reasons why it seems to me that rural constituencies should generally be smaller in population than urban ones. One is that, generally speaking, the organized pressure group in Canada is an urban phenomenon and, as we all well know, pressure groups to have a certain amount of influence on government policy. There are few such groups representing rural areas, since the more sparsely settled and agricultural areas of our country are not able generally to be so highly organized as our urban areas. Therefore boards of trade, chambers of commerce, industrial, social and other organizations tend to be urban-oriented and to represent the urban point of view. A member of parliament from an urban area is, therefore, complemented and supplemented in his activities by this kind of pressure group activity.
The other reason that comes to mind as to why we should have more members from rural than from urban areas is that the daily press is entirely urban, representing an urban point of view. To help counteract this there should be a few more members of parliament from rural areas. I am not suggesting, however, that there should be a great disparity such as we have today, either among urban areas or as between some rural areas and some urban areas. Indeed, as I mentioned earlier, whatever tolerance we choose is going to be such a change from what we have had


in the past, and will narrow the disparity so greatly, that this legislation will really be a revolutionary step forward.
Personally I would argue in favour of a tolerance of about 25 per cent, although I am not sure this is going to affect us very much. The way I have been working out the mathematics of the matter, those of us who represent rural ridings are going to represent about the same number of people whether the tolerance is 15, 20 or 25 per cent. The larger tolerance might, however, help hinterland constituencies and, of course, that would be an advantage to them.
These are the main points I wanted to bring out in this debate-the suggestion for the appointment of the commissioners on the various commissions, the argument that the rural-urban difference has been overplayed and that we should have been looking more at the great disparity between urban seats, the suggestion that there is some logic in keeping some disparity between urban ridings on the one hand and rural on the other and, finally, the argument that, although it may not make a substantial difference, if it would make all of us happy, a tolerance of 25 per cent would in my view at any rate, be feasible.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF COMPULSORY ARMED SERVICE
SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF COMPULSORY ARMED SERVICE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of adopting compulsory service in this country for all men 18 to 21 years of age, the service duration to be approximately 12 months.

He said: Mr. Speaker, one of the problems which are causing us great concern in the period we are going through at the present time is the problem of our youth, of those coming after us, who will assume the numerous responsibilities in an increasingly troubled world.
I think we have an important duty to perform and that is to season our youth as much as we can in order that they will be well equipped to face the challenge presented by the second half of the twentieth century.
In this confused world, often affected by internal divisions and a bit lost in the midst of ideologies feared by the average man, our youth do suffer psychologically in this ever changing modern world of ours.

Whether they be parents or public men, they all have some apprehension with regard to the future of our young people, wondering what those young people really want. They wonder about their hopes and yearnings and sometimes would gladly go back a generation or two to try and find the means to prevent an emancipation which is causing so much worry.
I appeal to all the people in Canada, to every parent and every politician, and I say to them that it is everybody's responsibility to consider the situation with the utmost care. We should do so in the most objective manner, trying to see whether our methods of training and education answer our present needs. Putting aside all emotionalism, we should take the trouble to consider every available possibility which might result in giving our children a better chance.
Mr. Speaker, in submitting a motion on compulsory service, on national service, or on compulsory military training-call it what you will-I never intended to stop our young people from becoming more independent, or even to slow down this development, because I am one of those who believe that there is nothing to be done against evolution. We have to live in the present, and look for solutions to the problems facing us today, as they are, and with the philosophy of 1964. Yet, I wonder whether our children themselves, without quite realizing it, do not suffer from that transformation of the family, from the changes in their social background, where each of us is concerned with his own problems, where the woman is less a mother than a wife, a man less a father than a husband, and, I would add, where the daughters and sons are not so much submissive children as members of a student group or the new trend among the young people of throwing everything overboard.
Even if there is no question of stopping their newly acquired freedom or an evolution which is in keeping with the times, I think that it is the responsibility of each and everyone of us-whether we be heads of families, politicians, or Canadian citizens-to meet the problem and see whether our young people have all the means available to help them attain their full development, as well as all institutions required to protect them against themselves.
I do not want to embark upon a full discussion of the educational problem, but, on the basis of various views expressed in various quarters, and of my own experience, I may,
I think, draw some conclusions and believe that some kind of compulsory service might become an additional factor, a formative element to help our young people prepare themselves better for life. To my mind, such 20220-52
Compulsory Armed Service service would give them, in a comparatively short period, an opportunity of meeting, so to speak, the tests of life, away from the protective action of their own people, or from their childhood friends and also, which is important, far from that little kingdom which each individual tries to create around himself. The young man would live in an age group society, where each one would be on his own in a struggle for and against himself, while having to bear and tolerate those with whom he would have to rub shoulders.
A strict discipline, a team experience where the authorities' decisions are imposed upon the group with no opportunity to discuss them, that is a phase which will become in itself an apprenticeship for this world, where we have to face so many hardships and inconveniences and which remains for each individual a continuous struggle.
Mr. Speaker, it might be difficult to put into words what a person gets from a military and rigid discipline, but experience has proven that it may have beneficial effects. Ask those who have done military service, inquire of the parents of youth who were in the cadet corps, take a look at our military colleges (even our parish guards) and you will realize that the results are nevertheless conclusive.
My years of militia service gave me the opportunity to acknowledge many such facts and to realize how much four hours of service each week can benefit those who will take the trouble to give up a few hours of leisure. And here, I venture to add, for those who think the army is a place where young people go astray, that our military force is not a place of perdition any more than bowling-alleys, restaurants, theatres, uncensored television and even some beatnik or bearded-people clubs.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe in the advantages of such a project and I appeal to everyone. I urge them to discard their prejudices and to take into serious consideration what compulsory service could mean for our country. I should like them to study my idea of such a service and, after full consideration, to look for ways which would enable the government of Canada to carry out such a project for the good of all young Canadians and with a view to greater national unity.
Since I have relatively little time at my disposal, to explain that project, I should like to list the most important points which deserve consideration by all the groups which form our population.
First of all, I would ask you to remove the word "conscription" from your minds, because many people associate it with world conflicts, wars, and general restrictions and

Compulsory Armed Service
sacrifices. The purpose of my scheme is of a social rather than a military character, and the armed forces would only be an instrument used to carry it out. Service would be in Canada only and our youth would never be sent to foreign countries, even for peacekeeping operations.
Some people say that our country's image abroad would suffer. I should like to give them certain examples of countries that have always been considered as most pacific; Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark and Ireland, where military service for young people has always existed.
A while ago, I referred to military colleges and I should like to come back to them briefly to try and show you that, while endeavouring to instil a spirit of discipline and respect for authority, even a sense of responsibility, through physical and military training, it remains possible to devote most of the time to education. As a matter of fact, our military colleges are to be commended because they succeed in giving a university training and in producing men with backbone and guts, men who can take their responsibilities. I do not see why the same principle could not apply to general service across the country.
What would stop this service from becoming a contribution to national unity and a means of spreading bilingualism and acquainting people with both basic cultures in the country? I see there a possibility of organizing the largest language school which would be available for all young Canadians. They would also have the advantage of visiting the country, of developing broader viewpoints and of knowing others their own age, who belong to different ethnic groups, all those who, tomorrow will take the place of their predecessors, and face this responsibility and challenge of developing and improving this country of ours.
People often complain that our schools do not give enough attention to Canadian history and politics. Well, this might perhaps be taken into account in the establishment of the programs. There also we find infinite educational possibilities which, I know, would raise problems of jurisdiction, but which are nevertheless worth studying, and I mean by that the possibility of postgraduate work to complete the studies already begun: study of a trade, technical studies, arts, letters, physical education, and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to the question of the students who wish to continue their studies after high school. In my plan, as you may have noticed, I provide for a 12-month service between the ages of 18 and 21 years, that is, within a period of five years, and this in order to allow, first of all, those who wish
[Mr. Laniel.l
to complete their high school to do so before being called up. As for the others who decide to continue their studies, in university or specialized schools, I would imagine a two or three-month service during two consecutive summers, with pay, in addition to service of the C.O.T.C. type (without pay) during the school term between the two summer service periods. Thus, nobody's studies would be affected, and I even wonder whether it would not prove an incentive to high school students to complete their studies at least, if not to further them.
Mr. Speaker, it could bring about beneficial effects for the Canadian economy, more especially as regards unemployment. After a study of statistics, I came to the conclusion that approximately 150,000 young men would be affected by this service every year. Excluding those who would complete their studies, as well as those who would fail the physical examination, a little over 100,000 would be removed from the labour market, thus contributing to reduce by 1 to 1| per cent the rate of unemployment in Canada. Out of those 100,000 and over, about 85 per cent are employed at present, and their jobs would become available for older workers. As for the 15 per cent of unemployed, what difference would there be in paying them an allowance for a national service, or in paying them unemployment insurance benefits, unemployment assistance or social security allowances?
According to average figures for 1956, 1961 and 1963, the percentage of young men out of work from 18 to 21 years of age is more than double the rate for the total labour force. Draw some parallels and ask yourselves what the government has to pay to initiate measures or incentives in orders to promote the economy and check unemployment. I had neither the means nor the necessary time at my disposal to study the matter thoroughly, but I would refer you to starred question No. 101 put by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) concerning the employment program for older people, in addition to the answer given as reported in Hansard of March 9 on page 675. When only the publicity costs of such a program are considered, the total amount reaches $199,511 and this only for 468 workers up to January 31, 1964. Since the program has been extended up to the end of March, this number should double and perhaps about a thousand persons will take advantage of this program.
That means the government will also have to pay for each of those individuals a monthly payment of $75 or an amount of $900 during the current year. This amount, multiplied by 1,000 people, gives a total of $900,000.

Once you add this total to the publicity expenses, you get a lump sum of about $1,100,000 and this, I repeat, without making any allowance for administration expenses. This fact among many others, goes merely to prove that the government has its heart set on giving work to the Canadian people and to show at the same time that if we are ready to spend millions for plans of this kind, I cannot see why we should refuse these millions for plans of this kind, I cannot see why we should refuse these millions to our young people, upon whom depends Canada's future; in a roundabout way the rest of the population would profit by it, as regards our serious unemployment problem.
And what about the savings effected by the unemployment insurance fund that would pay
100.000	benefits less than it does now, which, after all, represents $150 million a year?
One of the main objections comes from those who claim that our country cannot afford the prohibitive cost of such a service, for it is said that the cost might reach the half billion mark and even more. I made a few inquiries, and it is up to you to play about with these figures and see for yourselves if, in some instances, enough money could be saved, particularly after the tabling of the white paper, by the Minister of National Defence, and if there are any ways and means of avoiding undue expenditures, which might bring about administrative deficits.
First, we must consider what pay these young trainees should receive. Should it compare to the $112 paid monthly at present to new recruits; or, considering that the trainee would not embrace a military career, where hazards may be great, should the pay be based on an annual salary of say, $1,000, that is approximately $20 a week? If there were
100.000	young men in our armed forces and if each of them got $1,000, the total pay would amount to $100 million. To that must be added the cost of the training and administrative personnel, that is approximately $80 million, as well as the expenditures for maintenance, transport, food, clothing, hospitalization, etc. which would reach an estimated $120 million. The total cost would therefore be $300 million. Out of that sum, I think we could save about $40 million through the abolition of the militia. I therefore conclude that the establishment of compulsory service in Canada would cost between $250 and $300 million, an amount not quite so high as some people claim. Yet, I feel that the advantages we could derive from such a scheme certainly justify further consideration.
Mr. Speaker, on what basis do we decide that something is expensive? Is price the
20220-52i
Compulsory Armed Service only criterion or must we consider the value of what we are getting for our money? Considering that our first duty, as Canadians, and Canadians from every province, is to pave the way for our young people in giving them the best tools to face the difficulties of life, I come to the conclusion, in all sincerity, that such an expense is justified and that we must consider that matter most seriously.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to all members, judging from my own experience in the past three weeks, that the people's reaction have been very good, even among the young, even among most of the members of this house; I would add that such a favourable reaction, even in Quebec, is the evidence that Canadian unity is gaining ground, and that at home as well as elsewhere, we believe in a sense of national responsibility in view of the present difficulties. We are not afraid any longer to lose our French Canadian entity.
It is only if we decide to solve together our common problems-the problem of our young people is one of them, Canadian unity is another-that the dialogue will really be open and that we will come out of it better men, to serve a stronger Canada in a climate of better understanding. I do not want to mention here all the evidence that reached me but I will tell you that my mail runs almost 80 per cent in favour for the whole of Canada, against 70 per cent in Quebec. That means something.
Here is conclusive evidence to show you the evolution that has taken place in my own riding on a question which, a few years ago, met with much opposition. At the referendum held in April 1942, the county of Beau-harnois-Salaberry voted against the government proposal by 20 against 3, while today on two opinion programs on the local radio, more than 80 per cent of those who phoned were in favour of the setting up in our country of a compulsory service for young people. And the great majority see in such an instrument an additional way, and one of the most vital, to imbue our young people with a sense of responsibility and everything related to it. I admit that all are not agreed on the formula which I am proposing. Some would like a longer service, others do not want it under a military control, and a very small number prefer it to be voluntary; but almost everybody believes in the need of something similar to a military service and is of the opinion that the government, with the help of our institutions, should undertake a careful study of the question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was really astonished when I read this motion, for I was unaware that the hon. member for Beauhar-nois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) had such a warlike spirit.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this motion reduces itself to conscription of youth in peacetime. The play on words we got from the hon. member reminded me of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King who, at the outbreak of war, said it was mobilization and not conscription.
The hon. member spoke of unemployment, implying that compulsory military service would help to solve this problem in our country. I wonder whether this is a confession coming from a government member who, losing confidence in his own ministers, tells us that, after all they are unable to settle the question of unemployment otherwise than by conscription or compulsory military training of Canadian youth.
I also wonder whether that notice of motion has not been inspired by the government itself, through the medium of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry, to bring about the conscription of our young people. Personally, I am in favour of voluntary military service; let our young people decide for themselves whether they wish to join the armed forces, during the holidays or otherwise.
As a matter of fact, I think it would be preferable for the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin), who is in this house at this time, to ask the few-and I repeat the few-French speaking senior officers who are very well paid, to visit the universities, the high schools or classical colleges and to tell those young people that there is room for them in the federal civil service, in the national defence department and in the armed forces.
To my mind, this would encourage the younger men, without coercing them into anything; in other words, they could be guided towards a military career.
It is recognized by everyone that within the framework of our federative system, education is under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The education of youth is also under provincial jurisdiction of the provinces. Parents carry the responsibility of educating their children, but teachers and schools share this responsibility. If the hon. member wants our youth to be better trained, he should persuade the present government to decentralize, from the fiscal point of view, in order to grant provinces larger sources of income, thus allowing greater development in sports education, while encouraging better training for the young.

We hear people say that world tension is easing. We speak of peace. An encyclical letter has even been written on the subject. Many countries do not have compulsory service, and I have learned recently that even England does not have one.
I wonder then if instead of establishing compulsory military service in peacetime, it would not be better to encourage those Canadians-particularly French Canadians since relatively few of them hold key positions in our three armed services-who have a wish and a natural bent for it, to choose a military career. As a matter of fact, I would ask the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry if he does not feel that the government should encourage young French Canadians to play their rightful part in the Department of National Defence because, at the present time, there are only about 8 per cent of French Canadians in the department earning $5,000 or more.
I wonder also if it would not be possible to have orders given in both official languages in our armed forces.
Furthermore, I feel that a four-year course should be given at the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean so as to put it on the same footing as the Kingston military college. It could even be affiliated with the University of Montreal, as recommended by the St. Jean Baptiste society.
As for the children of French speaking members of our military personnel who serve overseas, I feel they should be educated according to the system in force in Quebec instead of under the Ontario system.
Mr Speaker, I wonder whether it would be possible to change our military uniforms so as to prevent any confusion with the armed forces of other countries.
The hon. member has quoted figures concerning the approximate cost of compulsory service. He mentioned pay but he forget to mention the cost of lodging, transporting, clothing and feeding the young people who would be forced to undergo military training.
That is my personal opinion, Mr. Speaker. I respect the feelings of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry, even if I do not share them. However, I must say that I am strongly against any form of peacetime conscription such as the one proposed by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry as long as such schemes bear any similarity to the one enforced by Mackenzie King.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the very start of my remarks, I would like to congratulate the hon. member from Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) for his courage in submitting his motion. Considering that, in the past, the people of Quebec were always, in a general way, systematically

opposed to military service, I think that a French speaking member from Quebec should be commended for his daring and courage in suggesting such a measure, even by those who do not necessarily agree with him in this respect.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we are dealing today with a rather delicate matter which has been fully discussed in the past, and was mostly carried into an entirely different field than the one for which it was intended. As a matter of fact, the emotional element prevailed in those discussions, feeling, rather than fact being primarily considered. To my mind, emotions were stressed and played upon.
A compulsory system would certainly have some advantages. On the other hand, we should also consider its drawbacks. I listened with great attention to the hon. member's argument in support of his motion, as well as to the remarks of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). At that time, I began to ponder on the political basis of Canada, and I realized how much the Liberal party and its military concepts had evolved over the years.
I think we still have in mind those famous political struggles during the 30 years following the first world war, and more particularly the famous conscription which was passed in 1917, and became the theme of all Liberal election campaigns thereafter. Indeed, resorting to demagogic means the Liberals always succeeded in striking political capital from the conscription issue in 1917, emotionally appealing to the people of Quebec, in order to be returned to power in Ottawa.
But in 1964, we see a member of the Liberal party suggesting in this house, the adoption of compulsory military service in this country.
I am not systematically opposed to the hon. member's motion, but I am trying to find out what would be gained or lost, or what would have to be paid for any gain.
I wondered whether, instead of having a compulsory military system, it would not be better to incorporate some measures of military training education in our secondary and university courses through the provincial educational system, which would inform Canadian citizens in matters of national defence, train them in the handling of arms in keeping with the present military evolution in the world, in which active military forces would be less and less needed. Moreover, in case of a conflict breaking out in some part of the world, or even in our own country, it would be well to count on part of our population having some-though, I admit, inadequate- training, and some idea of the military point of view.
Compulsory Armed Service
Mr. Speaker, I do not know exactly how, at the provincial level, an educational program could be established that would incorporate military training, but I believe that instead of studying the possibility of having compulsory military service for all young Canadians, it would be better to consider this aspect of the problem.
The hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry made a statement to which I take exception. He spoke about the advantages such a system would bring, and he mentioned more particularly the economic advantage which would result, that is a reduction in the number of unemployed. Now, I am categorically opposed to military service for our Canadian fellow citizens in order to stop unemployment.
As the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, has pointed out, it is almost like admitting that a solution has not been found to the problem of unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, if really the only way to fight unemployment is to impose military service on our young people, we have fallen far short of our present duty. Of course, if our young people were offered optional service, I would see some advantages to it. On the other hand, a one year period of service could be devised for our young people between 18 and 21, for which they could register when it would suit them most, according to their studies, their profession, their marriage or other circumstances.
This training could be divided in four periods of three months each and take place in four different regions of our country. For instance, training would be held for three months in Alberta so that our young Canadians could become familiar with that part of our country, travel throughout Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, and get to know the geography of their country. A second period of training could take place in Ontario and in the western part of that province. Thus, the recruits could visit Ontario and Manitoba. A third period of training could be held at Valcartier, in central Quebec, where our fellow citizens of other provinces could get acquainted with the ways and customs of the province of Quebec and perhaps appreciate them more. The final period of training would be in the maritimes so that they could get to know that part of the country better.
Military service in Quebec would also tend to promote the knowledge of French among English speaking Canadians. The training could be entirely in French, so that young Canadians doing their military service in Quebec for three months could mix with French Canadians and, in some way, be influenced by the people with whom they would have to live, as well as through their contacts, their visits and their training.

Compulsory Armed Service
Those are some of the benefits to be obtained from military service, though I do not feel it should be compulsory. It would have as a result to open new horizons for our youth, to take them away from their narrow bit of land so they could see the country as a whole, and avoid, if I may say so, a regional mentality which in fact warped our views of the Canadian government and of the principles which were at the basis for the setting up of this country.
It was said that in Canada, there is an alarming rise of juvenile delinquency and that military service might be a way to cope with that problem. There seems to be some truth in the allegation because, as far as I am concerned, young men from my riding who come to see me quite regularly ask for my assistance in order to be admitted to the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean or, into our armed forces generally speaking. There are even some older persons who were in the services before and would like to get back, because they were well treated and had an opportunity for growth.
There is a percentage of our citizens in Canada and in Quebec-I dare to say in Quebec-who would like to have the opportunity to do some military service in order to travel about the country and get some experience.
However, I do not think, as I said earlier, that to attain these worthy objects it would be necessary to have compulsory military service.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think that before action is taken the matter deserves much more consideration, because it involves several social, economics and even moral factors.
