speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was listening a little while ago to the hon. member for Beauharnois-Sala-berry (Mr. Laniel) outlining with a quaver in his voice the benefits for our Canadian youth of compulsory military service in our country. He mentioned for instance the troubled world in which we live, where youngsters having a hard time finding a situation, and he claimed that, with compulsory military service, the government would look after this guidance. He told us also that military service would give our young people training and discipline. He said also that, in his opinion, his motion would help stem unemployment in Canada.
Afterwards, he made a plea for all hon. members of the house to co-operate with him and face the problem with courage and boldness so that our youth will be able to attain self-achievement. He even urged us not to be afraid to lose our seats, but to take a

stand in favour of compulsory military service between the ages of 18 and 21. He gave us his conception of such a service, but it is not necessarily that of the hon. members, and especially not that of our group.
His notice of motion refers to compulsory service. We have always had military service in Canada, but not compulsory military service. He wants to impose upon our young men of 18 to 21 the obligation of doing military service or some other service for the government.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member also told us that since he had put his notice of motion on the order paper he had received numerous letters of congratulations from all the Canadian provinces, and especially from Quebec, and that 70 per cent of our young people would be anxious to see such service.
Mr. Speaker, whether such a service would cost $200 or $300 million, that is quite immaterial to us. Even though it would cost $1 billion.
The point I want to stress is the matter of compulsory service. We have had compulsory service in the past. As the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm pointed out a while ago, the Liberals kept themselves in office for 30 years by saying they were against compulsory service or conscription. Today, we have one of their own people proposing that we have compulsory service.
Personally, I have never been against- neither has anybody in Canada, I do not think-a young man joining the armed forces, as long as he does so voluntarily.
It is through persuasion, education and belief that young men finally become interested in the service, whether it be military or otherwise. I have no objection to that. But I am against any form of compulsory service.
There are some examples in Canada. It is not only compulsory or military service which provides educational facilities to our young men or enables them to acquire a sense of discipline. There are schools where attendance is not compulsory. We have here a member, the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde), who has looked after the recreational activities of young people in Quebec city for ten or 12 years, in connection with playgrounds and disciplinary training. No one was compelled to join that organization, but if they went there, it was because they were eager to acquire an education. By doing so, the member for Quebec West was offering his services, voluntarily, there was nothing compulsory involved.
Mr. Speaker, we are certainly not in favour of this notice of motion which I am convinced is a direct encroachment on education of our young men from 18 to 21 years of age, again an intrusion of the state at that level.

Mr. Speaker, it has been said that such a measure would check unemployment by compelling our young people to do military service, in order to vacate jobs and to enable older workers to get employment. Would such a measure give enough jobs to cope effectively with unemployment? I do not believe that such a measure would be likely to check unemployment and there are other ways to achieve it.
Mr. Speaker, after the war, we still had thousands of young people in the forces and we started immediately to have unemployment, although the number of our young people in the army was still quite high. Compulsory military service is certainly not the way to alleviate unemployment in this country. There are better solutions than that.
As far as we are concerned, we are offering a solution that the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Salaberry has not seen fit to accept yet but that many people, even the economists, accept more and more every day: that is to put our economic system at the service of our Canadian consumers.
With regard to our children's education, I think that we, fathers and mothers, can give some direction to our young between 18 and 21, telling them where to go or not to go, what to do or not to do, without any interference from any government whatsoever. We want our young people, our own children, to have a good future. We want to create an economic climate in which they can grow with complete freedom, without any obligation from anywhere, through education and persuasion alone. I sincerely believe that the fathers and mothers who talk with their chilren are the first who can have some influence on these young people and convince them by persuasion, dialogue, and belief as the hon. member said a while ago. There is no need for anything compulsory, or for military service.
Mr. Speaker, this is the solution we are suggesting and, as I said earlier, it is more and more acknowledged, even by economists. 1 have here a small English book entitled:

The problem, therefore, is not simply one of providing against old age, ill-health or temporary unemployment-essential though these safeguards will continue to be. We must visualize a situation when it would be impossible to provide "gainful" employment for a substantial and growing section of the population.

And it is in accordance with one of those points that the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry now brings forward his notice of motion, to take care of the unemployment problem in Canada.
I continue:

We are of the opinion that it would be foolish to attempt to retard or reverse this tendency; rather should we look upon it as a challenge and an opportunity-a challenge to solve the economic, social and moral problems, and an opportunity to move on into these wide fields of human endeavour that can only be explored on a voluntary basis.
The evil of unemployment resides in two things- poverty due to lack of access to the real wealth produced by the economic system, and misuse of the leisure it provides. The first can be cured by a reformed monetary system and the second, given the removal of the first, is the responsibility of the moral leaders of society, and of course of the individual himself.

Mr. Speaker, we do not support at all this measure intended to set up compulsory military service and I have said why. We are in favour of education, yes. We are in favour of persuasion, yes. We are in favour of guidance for our young people, but we do not need a strait-jacket to tell our children where they must go in life and in the future of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I shall now speak in the other official language of this country-

In order that there will be no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, may I say that my colleagues and I are completely opposed to this resolution, and included among our members are some who are veterans of war service or of military service after the war. There is no great public demand for compulsory service I was surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who said that the resolution might have been inspired by the cabinet. It might have been an interesting experience if other members of the official opposition had risen to speak today, and we had had the opportunity to see how many members on the government side would have spoken on the matter.

Compulsory Armed Service
There has been no demand for compulsory service, and not even the Royal Canadian Legion, which I believe has made demands of this sort in past years, has made any such demand in recent years. I was looking over their 1962 resolutions and they just ask for service in the reserves, while in their submission to the government last year there was no mention of compulsory service at all.
Some of the aims that the hon. member has in mind may be quite laudable. We want to do something for Canadian youth, but I think he is seeking to go about it in the wrong way. If we were to have such a program it would mean spending a considerable amount of money and I can think of many better uses for that money in helping our youth. For example, the Royal Canadian Legion is now operating a very good nationwide sports program to train athletes and to provide recreation for young people. I suggest that money might be given for that purpose instead of being used for compulsory service. I believe that the national advisory committee on physical fitness is meeting at the present time in Ottawa, and I suggest that more money could be given to that organization for its purposes.
With regard to the contribution to national unity which the hon. member mentioned, there are various organizations working towards this end now. I think of the organization called "Interprovincial Visits" which arranges visits between English speaking and French speaking students, so one will have a chance to see how the other lives. We might give more aid by way of a grant to this organization and achieve the same purpose that the hon. member has in mind.
In his own province of Quebec a department of youth was established a number of years ago. I am not sure whether this has been done anywhere else but it seems like a very good idea. I suggest that there ought to be such departments in other provinces, and that in the interests of the youth of our country the federal government could participate by assisting such departments with grants.
No substantial portion of the population is demanding compulsory service and in our opinion it would serve no useful purpose. In fact, at the present time the trend in the world is away from compulsory service. While we agree with some of the aims the hon. member has in mind, these aims can be much better achieved by grants to sports organizations, and organizations which promote visits of young people between provinces. Compulsory service would certainly be no solution

Mr. Speaker, in the very few moments left I wish to go on record as being opposed to this resolution. I am opposed on several grounds, but the short time left to me does not give me the opportunity to list them all. I am opposed because of the astronomical cost that would be involved, because of the effect on Canada's external relations and because I cannot see any real military value.
In so far as cost is concerned, if we assume that each of these young men between the ages of 18 and 21 who is inducted will receive $3 a day, which is double what a trained soldier got some 20 years ago, that would be $21 a week for each one. If we take a figure of 598,000 males from 18 to 21 and leave out some 15 to 18 per cent who would not be able to qualify because of medical reasons, there would still be approximately half a million, and even at a cost of $1,000 each per year we would have $500 million just for pay alone. Then we would have to have extra barracks. We would have to have additional administration staff and the total cost would probably be $700 million or $800 million a year.
A country like Malaysia which has instituted the draft had a reason for doing so. They are faced with a threat from Indonesia and just this week have had to introduce a draft system. It must also be remembered that a war no doubt would be a conventional war, if it should develop between these two countries. But Canada is in a different position. According to the 1963 figures we have an army of 49,381 men, and certainly to spend another $700 million or $800 million a year on inductees does not make economic sense.
So far as Canada's external relations are concerned, I would point out that at this time tensions generally between the major powers seem to be easing and I submit this would not be the time to go ahead and institute compulsory military training in Canada. The old idea of the Greeks, that every citizen should serve his city, is a fine idea, but it does not make practical sense today.
